newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani investors once bitten, twice shy.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani investors once bitten, twice shy.

text.p: Pakistani investors, hit by losses in big speculative stocks in recent weeks, are now being extra cautious, analysts said on Tuesday.

Former Karachi stock exchange president Yasin Lakhani said local investors had been demoralised by a lack of institutional support and the behaviour of the 100-share index, which closed at 1,525.03 points on Monday, down from 1,574.70 on March 31.
"We are now following the index and the buying and selling activities of foreign investors," Lakhani said.

Dealer Azhar Batla of Taurus Securities agreed that foreign investors were setting the pace in generally lacklustre trading, while their local counterparts were content to buy in the morning, sell in the afternoon and book small profits.

"Nowadays we don't see bullish sentiment from domestic financial institutions or hear local investors raise their voices," he said. "A local investor cautiously buys or sells if a foreign buyer lifts or hammers a particular stock."
"The market is trading at lower levels, but upward movement looks difficult due to the emergence of heavy selling on any appreciable rise," dealer Zubair Elahi said.
He said the market would go on trading in a narrow band, showing minor interest in inactive investment stocks.
The index rose 7.91 points, or 0.52 percent, to 1,532.94 at noon on Tuesday on short-covering in blue chips, but dealers said there was little genuine enthusiasm.

"It is a stagnant market. Trading volume has shrunk because there is no investor interest," dealer Hina Akhlaq said. "Their confidence has been shaken because of the country's economic troubles and activity revolves only around four or five scrips."
The Karachi bourse is dominated by trading in five major stocks: Pakistan Telecommunication Company Ltd, Hub Power Company, ICI Pakistan, FFC Jordan Fertiliser and Dewan Salman Fibre.
These have taken a beating this month in a market that has failed to respond to constitutional and economic reforms put forward by Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's government.

Sharif unveiled a package at the end of March designed to stimulate export-led growth by slashing taxes and tariffs. Early this month he used his huge parliamentary majority to remove the president's powers to sack an elected government.
Broker Majid Chapra said foreign investors might be waiting for the 1997/98 (July-June) budget to be announced in June.
